meta.title: Who really said "When I Read About the Evils of Smoking, I Gave Up Reading"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Joe E. Lewis. The joke was in print crediting Groucho Marx in 1950 — eight years before Lewis told his own, differently worded version.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'When I Read About the Evils of Smoking, I Gave Up Reading'?
meta.ogDescription: Joe E. Lewis gets the credit, but the joke was already in print under Groucho Marx’s name in 1950, and Lewis’s 1958 version is worded differently.

answer.label: Not Joe E. Lewis — actually Groucho Marx
answer.sourceLine: The joke is older than the man it is usually pinned on. Quote Investigator ↗ found it in the Hartford Courant on 7 July 1950, credited to Groucho Marx and aimed at smoking. Joe E. Lewis did tell a version — but not until 1958, and he told it differently: “Like I’ve been reading about how dangerous smoking is, so naturally I gave up reading.” Between those two dates the gag also ran under the names of a British MP and the comedian Phil Harris. Lewis was a late teller of a joke already in circulation.

source.heading: Where the joke actually starts

docMeta.dd: The Hartford Courant, “Informing You” by M. Oakley Stafford
7 July 1950, page 24 — credited to Groucho Marx
Reported speech, not a verbatim quotation
30 September 1958, Omaha World Herald — eight years later, different wording

source.excerpt: Groucho Marx says he became disturbed over the effects of smoking, after reading an article on the subject, he gave up reading. (That’s right, not smoking. That’s Groucho.)
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ dates the earliest instance to the Hartford Courant of 7 July 1950, where the joke is about smoking and is credited to Groucho Marx. Its conclusion is that Groucho “crafted the first instance in this family of humorous remarks by 1950” — with the standard caveat that earlier instances may yet turn up.

The same article shows the gag passing through several hands before Lewis: a version told in the House of Commons in March 1954 and credited there to Henry G. Strauss, and a drinking variant credited to the comedian Phil Harris in August 1955.
Joe E. Lewis appears in QI’s chronology only at 1958, in the Omaha World Herald, and the wording attributed to him there is not the wording that circulates under his name today.

Neither comedian’s Wikiquote page carries the line: it is absent from Joe E. Lewis ↗ and from Groucho Marx ↗, so the attribution rests on the newspaper record QI assembled rather than on any curated collection.
source.excerptNote: The 1950 Hartford Courant item as Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes it. Note that it is the columnist describing the joke, not Groucho’s own sentence — so even the earliest instance is a report, and the tidy one-line form everybody now quotes is a later polish that no source pins on anyone in particular.

source.rightsNote: The exact sentence on this page — the tidy modern one-liner — matches no traced publication, so there is no work whose rights we could report. The nearest documented ancestor is a 1950 newspaper column, which is well after the 1931 United States public-domain cut-off and therefore not safe to treat as free. We assert no rights status here: unknown, not open.

author.heading: About Groucho Marx
author.metaLine: 1890–1977 · American comedian, actor and quiz-show host
author.bio: Groucho Marx (2 October 1890 – 19 August 1977) was the wisecracking third Marx brother, who worked vaudeville, Broadway and film before hosting the quiz show You Bet Your Life. His trade was the fast one-liner, which made him both a prolific source of jokes and a permanent destination for other people’s.

misattribution.heading: Who has been credited with it
misattribution.intro: This is a joke that has changed owners repeatedly, which is the usual signature of a line nobody can prove they wrote first.

items.why: The Hartford Courant of 7 July 1950 credits him, in reported speech, with giving up reading rather than smoking — the first instance Quote Investigator ↗ could locate.
A version reached the House of Commons in March 1954, where Strauss attributed it to an unnamed American rather than to himself, as QI documents ↗.
A columnist credited the singer and comedian with the drinking version in August 1955 — the point at which the joke split into two topics, per QI ↗.
The name now attached to it. He told a version in 1958, eight years after the joke was already in print, and his reported wording differs from the line quoted under his name, according to QI ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: On the evidence Quote Investigator ↗ assembled, the joke belongs to Groucho Marx by 1950. Joe E. Lewis told it well, and late.

context.heading: How a joke changes hands
lead: Nothing about this line was ever written down as a quotation. It entered print in 1950 as a columnist’s paraphrase, got retold in Parliament, drifted from smoking to drinking, and only later settled into the crisp one-sentence shape people repeat now.

Joe E. Lewis ended up with the credit because he was the right kind of famous for it — a nightclub comedian whose public character was built on drinking and dangerous living. A joke about ignoring health warnings had nowhere better to land.
detailsBody: QI’s chronology runs: 1950 Groucho Marx (smoking, Hartford Courant); 1954 the House of Commons via Henry G. Strauss; 1955 Phil Harris (drinking); 1955 a newspaper cartoon caption; 1957 an anonymous “heavy cigaret smoker” in a Massachusetts paper; 1958 Joe E. Lewis.
Six owners in eight years, and the one whose name stuck was sixth. QI credits Fred Shapiro and Barry Popik for the underlying newspaper work.
context.pull: A joke about ignoring health warnings had nowhere better to land than a comedian famous for ignoring them.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the earliest instance to the Hartford Courant, 7 July 1950, page 24, credited to Groucho Marx, and concludes Groucho crafted the first instance by 1950.
Quote Investigator records Joe E. Lewis telling a version in the Omaha World Herald, 30 September 1958, worded "Like I’ve been reading about how dangerous smoking is, So naturally I gave up reading."
Quote Investigator records the 1954 House of Commons retelling credited to Henry G. Strauss and the August 1955 drinking variant credited to Phil Harris.
Groucho Marx lived 2 October 1890 to 19 August 1977 and was an American comedian, actor and game-show host.
Joe E. Lewis lived 12 January 1902 to 4 June 1971 and was an American nightclub comedian, actor and singer.
Wikiquote’s Joe E. Lewis page does not list this quotation.
The QI tag page for Joe E. Lewis links this investigation.
